This increase in marker loss seems to be due to an increase in whole chromosome loss, as all strains tested were homozygous in SNP-RFLP assays (Table S2). The bub1∆/∆ strain had similar URA3 marker loss rates to the mad2∆/∆ strain in the absence of fluconazole, and showed an elevated loss rate with fluconazole treatment, although the magnitude of increase was less than for the mad2∆/∆ strain (Figure 6C). We also measured the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) for MAD2, mad2∆/∆, and bub1∆/∆ strains using a broth dilution assay in RPMI. The MIC values were ≤0.125 µg/mL for the MAD2 strains. We observed MIC values of 0.125 and 0.25 µg/mL strains for the mad2∆/∆ and bub1∆/∆ strains. All of these values fall below the cutoff for fluconazole susceptibility of <8 µg/mL [34], but there was a trend towards increased MIC values in the mad2∆/∆ and bub1∆/∆ strains.

## 4. Discussion

In this work, we found that deletion of CaMAD2 decreased cell growth, increased marker loss rates, increased sensitivity to microtubule-destabilizing drugs, and increased sensitivity to DNA damage-inducing treatments. We did not see an increased requirement for CaMad2 when CSE4 was overexpressed resulting in additional kinetochore-microtubule attachments per centromere. Together, these results show that CaMad2 promotes genome stability at the chromosomal level through its canonical spindle assembly checkpoint roles and at the sub-chromosomal level through roles in preventing DNA damage and recombination. Additionally, CaMad2-GFP localized to dots, consistent with a role in kinetochore binding, and to the nuclear periphery, consistent with an additional role in DNA damage. We also found that, similarly to other strains with altered chromosome segregation checkpoint function, deletion of MAD2 increases growth on fluconazole, and that fluconazole treatment elevates whole chromosome loss rates in the mad2∆/∆ strain.

A prior characterization of CaMad2 found that it is important for accurate chromosome segregation, survival in high levels of hydrogen peroxide, and virulence in a mouse model of infection [19]. We found that deletion of MAD2 in C. albicans results in a slow growth phenotype. This is similar to previous observations that mad2∆ strains of the Fusarium head blight fungus Fusarium graminearum and the multinucleate fungus Ashbya gossypii had reduced growth and viability, likely due to high levels of aneuploidy [35,36]. Interestingly, haploinsufficiency was also observed in our experiments with C. albicans and in A. gossypii [35]. MAD2 haploinsufficiency also causes chromosome instability in human cancer cells and mouse embryonic fibroblasts [37], while overexpression of the MAD2 gene is also associated with tumor formation and poor cancer prognosis [38,39]. The phenotypes observed with both decreased and increased levels of MAD2 suggest that MAD2’s function relies on a particular level of expression in the cell. This may be related to the importance of the protein’s stoichiometry. Mad2 protein is found in both open and closed conformations, which dimerize to each other. This dimerization helps convert the open form into the closed form that then binds to Cdc20 to form the MCC [40]. Thus, up or down regulation of the protein may affect the stoichiometry and the amount of bound closed Mad2, which could disrupt the spindle assembly checkpoint.

Previously, Bai et al. showed elevated sorbose resistance rates and homozygosis of the mating type locus in strains lacking CaMAD2 suggesting that CaMad2 has roles in chromosome segregation accuracy in C. albicans [19]. The sorbose resistance assay measures monosomy of chromosome 5 due to the presence of multiple sorbose utilization genes on chromosome 5. We used selection of 5-FOA resistant colonies to measure loss of the URA3 marker gene. Since this assay requires loss of only a single gene, it can detect multiple types of loss of heterozygosity events. Interestingly, in strains lacking CaMAD2, we saw elevated URA3 marker loss rates. These elevated loss rates in rich media were primarily due to smaller-scale events, such as mutation and recombination, as all colonies were still heterozygous. Overall, these results show that deletion of CaMAD2 causes both chromosome loss phenotypes and elevated small-scale DNA changes.

Our treatment sensitivity assays also support a model where CaMad2 has roles in chromosome segregation and preventing DNA damage. We confirmed the sensitivity of strains lacking CaMad2 to 50 µM nocodazole, a microtubule destabilizing drug, in our experiments. Bai et al. showed reduced viability of strains lacking CaMad2 following short-term exposure to high concentrations (147, 88, and 33 mM) of hydrogen peroxide [19]. We tested longer-term exposures (24 h) to a lower concentration (1 mM) and also found sensitivity of strains lacking CaMad2 to this lower concentration, as demonstrated by reduced growth. The hydrogen peroxide results, together with the ultraviolet light sensitivity and increased URA3 marker loss due to recombination or other smaller scale events observed with the Camad2∆/∆ strain, demonstrate that CaMad2 also has a role in preventing DNA damage. Throughout our work, we saw similar phenotypes with Camad2 deletion and Cabub1 deletion strains, and in a few experiments, even saw stronger phenotypes with the mad2 deletion strain. Prior work in budding yeast and fission yeast found that bub1 mutants had more severe chromosome segregation defects than deletions of mitotic checkpoint components, such as Mad1, Mad2, and Mad3 [41]. There are several possibilities to explain why the phenotypes were more similar in C. albicans, including the presence of an H2A form that cannot be phosphorylated by Bub1 [17] and/or the important role of CaMad2 in DNA damage responses.

Additionally, prior work has shown that the nuclear periphery localization pattern of Mad2 is associated with the response to DNA damage [6]. The nuclear periphery localization pattern we observed with CaMad2 is consistent with the hypersensitivity to DNA damage and the high proportion of sub-chromosomal marker loss events. However, CaMad2 localization to the nuclear periphery appears to be the default location rather than a specific response to DNA damage, as the treatment with hydrogen peroxide did not increase the proportion of cells with a complete ring of CaMad2-GFP at the nuclear periphery. These results are also consistent with the result in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that Mad1 and Mad2 only bind to kinetochores when there is a problem with the spindle or kinetochore [42]. Together, these results indicate that the DNA damage response through Mad2 is conserved in C. albicans.

There are a few different proposed mechanisms in S. cerevisiae for the role of Mad2 in preventing DNA damage. Mad2 prolongs cell cycle arrest in cells with unrepaired double-strand breaks, suggesting that it may be important for allowing cells time to repair the DNA damage [43]. In S. cerevisiae, Mad2 also potentially has roles in nucleotide excision repair pathways, as mad2∆ shows synthetic lethality with the DNA damage response genes RAD10 and RAD23, which are subunits of nucleotide excision repair factor 1 and nucleotide excision repair factor 2, respectively [44]. Additionally, recent evidence shows that Mad2 promotes translation of the S-phase cyclins Clb5/6 and contributes to cell survival in response to replication stress when Rad53 is not functional [7]. In the future, it will be interesting to further characterize the mechanisms by which CaMad2 contributes to DNA damage responses in C. albicans.

It will also be critical to further explore the interactions between spindle assembly checkpoints and the development of drug resistance. Deletion of MAD2 increases sensitivity to antifungals that target microtubules, such as thiabendazole in C. albicans and F. graminearum [36], but deletion of CaMAD2 increases growth on the antifungal fluconazole. This observation is similar to other strains with altered chromosome segregation checkpoint function, including bub1∆/∆, sgo∆/∆, and h2a.2∆/∆ strains [17], suggesting that disruption of any of these genes may promote the evolution of drug resistance in C. albicans. Cells lacking CaMAD2 had slightly elevated MIC values relative to cells without disruption of CaMAD2, but both strains were still below the MIC cutoff for resistance. It would be interesting to test whether cells lacking CaMAD2 evolve fluconazole resistance differently than cells with functional CaMAD2 following repeated exposure to fluconazole.

Fluconazole resistance is associated with elevated levels of aneuploidy. In one set of clinical and laboratory strains, approximately 50% of fluconazole resistant strains contained a whole chromosome or segmental aneuploidy, while 10% of fluconazole sensitive strains were aneuploid [45]. We found that the elevated marker loss rate seen in rich media conditions with the mad2∆/∆ strain increases further upon exposure to treatment. Importantly, the type of marker loss events also changed from sub-chromosomal events to whole chromosome homozygosis, indicative of whole chromosome aneuploidy. Exposure to fluconazole induces aneuploidy through the separation of the nuclear membrane segregation and cytokinesis processes [46]. Our results show that the absence of CaMAD2 may potentiate fluconazole-induced aneuploidy, which leads to better growth on low levels of fluconazole for mad2∆/∆ strains.

## 5. Conclusions

In this work, we found that CaMad2 promotes genome stability through its direct spindle assembly checkpoint role in promoting accurate chromosome segregation and through reducing smaller scale chromosome changes due to recombination and DNA damage repair. Furthermore, the frequent nuclear periphery localization pattern of CaMad2-GFP is consistent with a role in DNA damage response as similar patterns have been seen in other organisms. Together, our results demonstrate that a Mad2-dependent DNA damage response is conserved in C. albicans. We also found that deletion of MAD2 increases growth on fluconazole similar to other strains with altered chromosome segregation checkpoint function. These results indicate that disruption of spindle assembly checkpoint genes, including MAD2, may promote the evolution of azole drug resistance in C. albicans.

## Abstract

Although loss of B cell tolerance, autoantibody production and immune complex deposition are hallmarks of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), CD8 T cell infiltration in the kidneys is the best predictor of poor prognosis in lupus nephritis, a severe manifestation of SLE. Here we examined the origin, differentiation, and functional consequence of CD8 T cells infiltrating kidneys in lupus-prone mice. TCF-1+ stem-like CD8 T cells in renal-draining lymph nodes underwent TCR-dependent, antigen-driven expansion with differentiation into cytotoxic kidney-infiltrating cells that promoted tissue injury contingent on CD4 T cell help, and IL-21 and IL-15 signaling. CD8 T cell differentiation was marked by persistent AP-1 activity and cytotoxic function despite increased expression of immune checkpoints. A parallel program of CD8 T cell differentiation in kidneys of patients with lupus nephritis reflected shared pathogenesis. Thus, a T cell differentiation program analogous to that in chronic infections and cancer is found in lupus; however, CD8 T cells in systemic autoimmunity retain effector function despite terminal differentiation.

## Abstract

Loss of B cell tolerance, autoantibody production and immune complex deposition are hallmarks of systemic lupus erythematosus. Al Souz et al. find that kidney-infiltrating CD8+ T cells differentiate from stem-like precursors in renal lymph nodes and cause tissue injury in lupus nephritis, demonstrating that pathological organ-specific responses mediated by stem-like CD8+ T cells are embedded within systemic autoimmunity.

## INTRODUCTION

Lupus nephritis is a severe manifestation of the autoimmune disease systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE, lupus) affecting the majority of patients1, often resulting in renal failure necessitating kidney dialysis or transplantation2. Lupus is characterized by loss of B cell tolerance with production of autoantibodies directed against DNA and nucleoproteins with autoantibody-autoantigen (immune) complexes depositing in tissues, particularly kidneys, followed by recruitment of immune cells and organ damage3,4. Circulating autoantibodies precede clinical symptoms by years and are not always predictive of disease5, highlighting incomplete understanding of disease mechanisms. Prevention of kidney damage by immunosuppression, including B cell depletion, a therapeutic mainstay, is achieved in less than half of patients6.

Although kidney immune complex deposition is a hallmark of lupus nephritis, immune cell infiltration is the best predictor of poor prognosis7–9, with over one-third of patients having persistent kidney immune cell infiltration that frequently leads to progressive tissue injury10–12. The presence of kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells correlates with adverse clinical outcomes, including progression to end-stage renal disease11,13–17. The contribution of CD8 T cells to tissue injury, along with their source and differentiation, remains incompletely understood. Lupus mouse models are powerful tools to uncover the pathogenic role of T cells in causation of organ damage, including mechanisms independent of injury induced by autoantibodies18,19. Secondary lymphoid organs, particularly draining lymph nodes, play a crucial role in immune responses, as they serve as the initial site of tissue antigen drainage through the lymphatic system20. This occurs in kidneys either through lymph flow to renal lymph nodes or indirectly through antigen acquisition by antigen-presenting cells, which migrate to the kidney21,22. Additionally, lymph nodes maintain prolonged memory response during chronic antigenic stimulation, as loss of homing of T cells renders them dysfunctional23.

Chronic antigen exposure in inflammatory settings results in generation of long-lived, hypofunctional CD8 T cells, referred to as stem-like, that are poised to replenish effector cells for tissue maintenance and pathogen control24. These cells respond to immune checkpoint blockade in cancer and arise during chronic infection, states of persistent antigen stimulation25,26. We hypothesized that an analogous program of CD8 T cell differentiation occurs in lupus in which chronic (auto)antigen stimulation is present, with stem-like CD8 T cells in lymph nodes serving as a reservoir to replenish tissue-damaging effector T cells27–31. If true, this would explain why kidney inflammation in patients persists during immunosuppression and is replenished after immunosuppression is stopped32,33. Analogizing these immune effector programs enables comparison of conserved pathways that incite tissue damage to better understand systemic autoimmunity.

Here we examined the origin, development, and function and kidney infiltrating CD8 T cells in murine lupus. We found that CD8 T cells caused kidney damage in lupus. Paired scRNA/scATAC showed that these CD8 T cells differentiated from stem-like precursors to cytotoxic and terminally differentiated cells that remained poised for effector function, with a parallel differentiation pathway in kidney biopsies from lupus nephritis patients. Differentiation and effector function of stem-like CD8 T cells depended on IL-15 signaling and CD4 T cell help via IL-21. Kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells were clonally expanded, originating from kidney-draining renal lymph nodes (rLN) with the spleen serving a throughway of T cell trafficking to kidneys. Using a TCR-signaling reporter lupus mouse, we determined that clonal expansion and cytotoxicity were TCR-dependent, consistent with kidney antigen-directed responses and preserved function despite terminal differentiation. Thus, cytotoxic T cell differentiation programs under chronic antigen stimulation are conserved in systemic autoimmunity. However, unlike in cancer and chronic infection, CD8 T cells retain effector function despite upregulation of immune checkpoint molecules perpetuating tissue injury. These findings improve understanding of T cell dysregulation in lupus.

## RESULTS

### CD8 T cells cause kidney damage in lupus nephritis

We characterized CD8 T cells from nephritic kidneys, spleen, and renal lymph nodes (rLN, the lymphatic drainage sites of kidneys) of lupus-prone MRL/MpJ-Faslpr/J (MRL/lpr) mice. Nearly all CD8 T cells in kidneys were CD44hiCD62Llo effector cells, while those in rLN and spleens were comprised of naïve, memory, and effector subsets (Fig. S1A,B). We found in spleens and rLN a dominant stem-like CD8 T cell population delineated by expression of TCF-1 and SLAM family member Ly108 (SLAMF6). In contrast TCF-1−CXCR6+ (Ly108−CXCR6+) cells were enriched in kidneys (Fig. 1A,B; S1C), reflecting differentiation and loss of stem-like state. We made similar observations in two other lupus-prone mouse models, NZB x NZW/F1J (NZBWF1/J) and C57BL/6J.Sle1.Yaa (B6.Sle1.Yaa), but not in C57BL/6 mice, indicating a lupus-specific effect across strains (Fig. S1D–K). Within kidneys, TCF-1−CXCR6+ CD8 T cells were enriched for granzyme B, consistent with cytotoxic function as cells differentiated from a stem-like state (Fig. 1C; S1L). Additionally, a larger proportion of kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells in comparison to cells from lymphoid tissues expressed PD-1 and Tim-3 (Fig 1D,E) indicating terminal differentiation following TCR engagement34, and CD69 and CD103 (Fig. 1F,G), markers of tissue resident memory T (Trm) cells indicative of prior activation and expansion35. Kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells accumulated as mice aged (Fig. S1M), with an increase in expression of PD-1 and Tim-3, and granzyme B (Fig. S1N,O). These changes correlated with increase in urinary protein:creatinine ratio, denoting progressive kidney injury (Fig. S1P).

To determine if CD8 T cells damaged kidneys, we antibody-depleted CD8 T cells from MRL/lpr mice. At end of treatment, there was reduction in number of circulating and kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells (Fig. 1H; S1Q) and CD4 T cells (Fig. S1R), albeit not complete loss, as deficient cell depletion occurs in murine lupus models due to defective phagocytic clearance of IgG-bound cells36. CD8 T cell depletion stabilized otherwise progressive kidney injury independently of circulating anti-dsDNA autoantibodies (Fig. 1I; S1S,T), whereas isotype control administration resulted in disease progression as reflected by increased urinary protein:creatinine ratio. CD8 T cells retained in the kidney after depletion continued to differentiate, with reduced Ly108+ cells and concomitant increase in CXCR6+ and CD69+CD103+ CD8 T cells despite overall reduction in their number (Fig. 1J; S1U).

### Terminally differentiated kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells maintain effector function

We assessed the effector function of PD-1+Tim-3+ kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells, markers of terminal differentiation associated with diminished function in cancer and chronic infection37–40. We sorted CD44hiPD-1+Tim-3+ CD8 T cells and their PD-1−Tim-3− counterparts from kidneys, finding increased granzyme B expression in the former (Fig. 1K). Upon restimulation, both subsets had comparable expression of IFNγ and TNFα (Fig. 1L). Neither subset had elevated Ki-67 expression (Fig. 1M), reflecting diminished proliferation potential of intra-renal CD8 T cells.

We next treated MRL/lpr mice with a PD-1 inhibitor antibody aimed at preventing CD8 T cell dysfunction following engagement of PD-L1. After 8 weeks of treatment, we did not observe differences in the frequency and number of kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells (Fig. S1V), which maintained expression of Ly108, CXCR6, TCF-1, granzyme B, IFNγ, and TNFα (Fig. S1W–Z). There was slight increase in the number of CD69+CD103+ CD8 T cells (Fig. S1X) in line with increased Trm formation findings following anti-PD-1 treatment41. PD-1 blockade did not aggravate kidney injury (Fig. S1AA), demonstrating that despite expression of PD-1 and Tim-3, kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells have persistent effector function unaffected by immune checkpoint blockade.

### Kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells arise from stem-like precursors and then differentiate

To characterize T cells in lupus nephritis, we sorted B220−CD4−CD8+ and B220−CD4+CD8− CD44hi cells from kidneys, spleens, and rLN of MRL/lpr mice for single-cell multiome to simultaneously capture chromatin accessibility and transcriptional profiles within the same cell (Fig. S2A,B). We identified ten subsets of kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells (Fig. 2A; S2C) based on RNA expression of T cell subtype-defining genes, comparing these results to those from B6 naïve cells to rule out contamination. Prominent clusters included stem-like, activated, innate-like, Trm, type I interferon-induced (ISG), cytotoxic, terminally differentiated, and proliferating, with overlapping CD8 T cell subsets present in spleens and rLN (Fig. S2C–G). We captured stem-like CD8 T cells in all three tissues, as evidenced by high Tcf7 expression (Fig. 2B; S4F–G) and enriched chromatin accessibility at Tcf7 binding motif (Fig. 2C; S4H–I). We also identified CD4 T cell subsets in kidney, spleen, and rLN classified into stem-like, memory (Tcm), cytotoxic, polarized (Th1, Th2, Tfh, and Treg), and proliferating CD4 T cells (Fig. S2J–P).

To understand CD8 T cell differentiation within the kidney, we built a chromatin accessibility-based differentiation trajectory using Monocle342. By sequentially selecting precursors with the highest similarity in chromatin accessibility, we identified stem-like CD8 T cells as precursors to cytotoxic and terminally differentiated kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells (Fig. 2D). We ranked cells from stem-like (low pseudotime) to terminally differentiated (high pseudotime) and performed differential transcription factor motif accessibility to determine cellular profiles during CD8 T cell fate transition. We identified Tcf7 and Lef1 as critical transcription factors that maintained a stem-like phenotype as evidenced by their upregulated motif accessibility, gene accessibility, and RNA expression (Fig. 2E–H), alongside upregulated accessibility and expression of other stem-like genes including Slamf6, Ccr7, Il7r, and Bach2 (Fig. 2F–H). Motif accessibility of AP-1 transcription factors (Fos, Jun) was upregulated early along pseudotime, followed by upregulation of transcription factors Tbx21 and Eomes (Fig. 2E). As cells differentiated, they upregulated accessibility and expression of genes denoting cytotoxicity and terminal differentiation (Fig. 2F–H), including Tox, Havcr2, and Pdcd1 which continued to increase as accessibility of Tcf7 and Slamf6 continued to decrease (Fig. 2I). Terminally differentiated cells maintained high Runx3, Gzmb, Ifng, and Ccl5 chromatin accessibility and RNA expression (Fig. 2H). These results suggested that upon AP-1 activation, stem-like kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells differentiated toward cytotoxic effectors regulated by Tbx21 and Eomes, which then progressed to a terminally differentiated state expressing Tox and immune checkpoint molecules. Yet, terminally differentiated kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells retained effector potential.

### Renal lymph nodes are the origin of kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells

We merged cells from spleen, rLN, and kidney to explore tissue-driven differences, and found that kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells clustered separately except for stem-like cells, suggesting stem-like CD8 T cell similarity across tissues (Fig. 3A,B). To identify distinct epigenetic states of kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells, we compared the chromatin accessibility profiles of transcription factor binding motifs (predicting binding activity) between stem-like and terminally differentiated cells across tissues. Among transcription factors, accessibility of AP-1 was upregulated in both stem-like (Fig. S3A) and terminally differentiated (Fig. S3B) kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells compared to counterparts in spleen and rLN, suggesting sustained AP-1 signaling independent of differentiation. Similarly, kidney-infiltrating CD4 T cells were phenotypically distinct from their counterparts in spleen and rLN (Fig. S3C,D) and had elevated AP-1 accessibility across differentiation states (Fig. S3E–H). These results suggest elevated AP-1 transcription factor activity in both CD8 T cells and CD4 T cells in nephritic kidneys, beginning in stem-like cells, persisting throughout differentiation, and failing to terminate despite upregulation of canonical inhibitory molecules.

To elucidate transcriptional program differences in CD8 T cells across tissues, we next performed Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) and found elevated expression of genes associated with TCR signaling in rLN CD8 T cells, especially in stem-like cells, compared to their spleen and kidney counterparts (Fig. 3C,D). By contrast, expression of gene programs downstream of TCR-mediated activation and inflammation, including AP-1 associated genes, IFNγ response, and TNFα signaling via NF-κB was elevated in kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells relative to counterparts in spleen and rLN CD8 T cells (Fig. 3C,D). These findings pointed towards TCR-dependent priming in the rLN, with TCR-activated stem-like CD8 T cells migrating to kidney where they continued to experience TCR signaling. Notably, TCR signaling was absent in most splenic populations, reflecting passive transit through the spleen.

We next applied unbiased Weighted Gene Correlation Network Analysis (WGCNA) to identify de novo co-regulated gene programs shared across tissues and distinct to kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells43, focusing on terminally differentiated cells in kidneys, spleens, and rLNs to control for stem-like or effector cells leaving lymphoid tissues. We identified an immune checkpoint gene program (Fig. 3E) with co-expression of immune checkpoint molecules Ctla4, Entpd1, Havcr2, and Lag3, and transcription factors Maf and Tox in terminally differentiated CD8 T cells across all three tissues. We further identified an activation gene program exclusive to terminally differentiated kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells (Fig. 3F), which, despite an elevated immune checkpoint gene program, continued to be significantly enriched compared to counterparts in the rLN and spleens. In line with increased AP-1 transcription factor activity and signaling in kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells (Fig. 3C,D; S3A,B), WGCNA identified co-expression of AP-1 genes (Fosb, Fos, Jun, and Junb) and Ifng, Ccl3, and Cxcr6 in kidney-infiltrating terminally differentiated CD8 T cells. These results suggested that kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells in lupus nephritis are continuously exposed to activation signals that counteract immunoregulatory programs typically associated with cessation of function in terminally differentiated cells.

We performed Gene Regulatory Network (GRN) analysis to identify transcriptional regulators that governed distinct gene expression profiles in kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells versus spleen and rLN counterparts. Across tissues, we identified Nr4a2 as a prominent transcriptional activator that correlated with elevated RNA expression of Pdcd1, Havcr2, Il10ra (Fig. 3G; S3I), suggesting Nr4a2 as a transcriptional regulator that shaped an exhaustion-like inhibitory program in terminally differentiated CD8 T cells44,45. Specific to kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells, we additionally identified Runx3 as a prominent transcriptional activator (Fig. 3G). Runx3 accessibility correlated with elevated RNA expression of Prf1, Nkg7, Il2rb, Cxcr6, Itga1, and Klrd1 in Trm and terminally differentiated cells (Fig. 3H), consistent with its roles in shaping cytotoxic effector function46,47 and tissue residency48.

### Stem-like CD8 T cells migrate from renal lymph nodes and differentiate within the kidney

Co-clustering of kidney, rLN, and splenic stem-like CD8 T cells suggested that stem-like cells migrate from lymphoid tissue to kidneys. We treated MRL/lpr mice with the S1PR1 agonist FTY720 to limit lymphocyte emigration from lymphoid tissue thereby preventing recruitment of cells into the kidney. As expected, circulating and kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells decreased following treatment (Fig. 4A), particularly in perivascular areas (Fig. 4B,C). Despite reduced recruitment, Ly108+ expression decreased and CXCR6+ expression increased (Fig. 4D), consistent with ongoing differentiation of kidney-engrafted stem-like cells. Consistent with these findings, most circulating cells in PBS-treated mice were stem-like (Fig. 4E) suggesting these CD8 T cells bridge lymphoid tissue to kidneys.

To ascertain the ability of stem-like cells to give rise to kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells, we adoptively transferred B220−CD45.1/1 Ly108+ stem-like CD8 T cells isolated from rLN into CD45.1/2 MRL/lpr mice, transferring CD45.1/1 CXCR6+ differentiated CD8 T cells as comparators (Fig. 4F; S4A). While both transferred populations were found in circulation 24h after transfer (Fig. S4B,C), only Ly108+ cells engrafted in recipient mice after 8 weeks (Fig. 4G,H; S4D). Transferred Ly108+ cells retained Ly108 expression in rLN but differentiated into CXCR6+ cells in kidneys, supporting rLN stem-like cells as the source of kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells (Fig. 4I). Donor cells, which had more recently immigrated to the kidney compared to pre-existing recipient cells, had higher co-expression of PD-1 and Tim-3 (Fig. 4J) despite comparable numbers (Fig. S4E). These findings indicated that kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells are derived from stem-like precursors in the rLN.

### Kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells arising from rLN are clonally expanded

To further investigate the origin of kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells, we performed paired scRNA/scTCR sequencing on spleen, rLN and kidney CD8 T cells from nephritic mice. Consistent with our single-cell multiome, cell subsets ranged from stem-like to effector/terminally differentiated cells and kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells, again clustered separately from their counterparts in rLN and spleens (Fig. 5A,B). There was notable expansion of kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells, with 15 of the top clones comprising approximately 40% of all clones (Fig. 5C) and a higher Gini index amongst kidney CD8 T cells, congruent with expansion of a small number of clones (Fig. S5A). These same clones were detected in the spleen and rLN. These results suggested that priming occurred in the rLN, after which the cells undergo clonal expansion, exit into circulation, and traffic through the spleen. We observed clonal overlap between kidney cluster 9, a stem-like kidney population, and other kidney clusters (clusters 2, 6–8), also supporting the role that stem-like CD8 T cells were migrating from lymphoid tissue to kidneys (Fig. 5D,E). Examination of the top 15 expanded clones within kidneys revealed shared clonality between all clusters, indicating a common origin (Fig. S5B), with dominant clones emerging across all clusters. Expanded clones were also more differentiated, expressing Tox, Pdcd1, Havcr2, Lag3, and Tigit, as well as continuous Gzmb expression (Fig. 5F). Expanded clones were not shared across mice (Fig. S5C), reflecting expansion in individual animals with no public clones; however, some clones did share Trvb genes (Fig. S5D). Taken together, this analysis revealed oligoclonal expansion of kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells, indicating antigen-specific response to kidney antigen(s) instead of non-specific activation.

We also examined clonal expansion of CD4 T cell subsets (Fig. S5E–G) which was ~10-fold less compared to expanded CD8 T cell clones (Fig. 5C; S5H). There was less tissue-specific expansion, with CD4 T cell clones equally expanded among rLN, spleens, and kidneys (Fig. S5I–J), with clonal overlap nonetheless suggesting stem-like origin of kidney-infiltrating CD4 T cells.

### Clonal expansion and differentiation of kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells is driven by TCR engagement

CD8 T cells can be activated by direct TCR engagement or in a TCR-independent manner, relying on toll-like receptors and cytokines49. To distinguish between these two possibilities, we generated Nur77-eGFP lupus-prone reporter mice (MRL/lpr.Nur77-eGFP) to assess direct TCR engagement50. Nur77 (encoded by Nr4a1) is expressed downstream of TCR signaling and is exclusively upregulated upon TCR engagement51. Kidney CD44hiCD8 T cells expressed eGFP (Fig. 5G), with eGFP+ CD8 T cells showing preferential expression of PD-1, Tim-3, and granzyme B compared to eGFP− counterparts from the same animals (Fig. 5H,I), reflecting cytotoxic potential upon differentiation following TCR engagement. eGFP+PD-1+Tim-3+ cells, representing terminally differentiated cells recently engaging antigen, retained proliferative potential in the spleen and rLN and cytotoxic potential in the kidney compared to their eGFP− counterparts (Fig. S5K). Thus, eGFP+ allowed us to compare antigen-activated CD8 T cells to bystander counterparts.

We next performed combined scRNA/TCR sequencing on sorted CD44hieGFP− and eGFP+ CD8 T cells from nephritic MRL/lpr.Nur77-eGFP mice (Fig. 5J; S5L). eGFP+ cells overlapped with eGFP− cells and were not exclusive to a given cluster (Fig. 5J,K). Yet, analysis of total clones showed preferential clonal expansion in eGFP+ versus eGFP− cells in all three tissue types, with increasing clonal expansion from the rLN to spleen and then kidney, consistent with rLN as a nidus of T cell activation (Fig. 5M). There was clonal overlap between eGFP+ cells across tissue types, with almost total overlap between splenic and kidney-infiltrating eGFP+ cells, suggesting that eGFP+ cells captured in the spleen were pre-selected and en route to kidneys (Fig. 5N), findings reflected by high Gini coefficients in spleen eGFP+ cells and kidney CD8 T cells (Fig. S5M). Comparison of the top 15 expanded clones showed a similar dynamic, with eGFP+ cells being more expanded than their eGFP− counterparts in each respective tissue (Fig. S5N). However, eGFP− clones largely overlapped with eGFP+ counterparts, suggesting prior TCR activation.

We also sought to compare differential gene expression between eGFP− and eGFP+ cells to investigate the effect of TCR signaling on CD8 T cell differentiation. Despite finding eGFP+ cells across all three tissues, Nr4a1 (encoding Nur77) in CD8 T cells was enriched in rLNs and kidneys compared to spleens (Fig. 5O), reflecting antigenic encounters in the former two organs, supporting the idea that rLNs were initial sites of stem-like CD8 T cells recruited into the kidney. We observed downregulation of stemness genes (Tcf7, Ccr7, Il7r) in eGFP+ cells compared to eGFP− counterparts, particularly in kidneys, with expression of genes associated with cytotoxicity (Prdm1, Gzmb) and further differentiation (Pdcd1, Havcr2) (Fig. 5P). This difference underscored TCR signaling in governing cytotoxic potential and by extension, the pathogenicity of kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells.

### CD4 T cell help is necessary for CD8 T cell-mediated kidney injury

It remained unclear whether CD8 T cells required CD4 T cell help to drive kidney injury. We transferred 3×106 total CD8, CD4, or CD8+CD4 T cells (1:1) into T-cell deficient lupus mice (MRL/MpJ-Faslpr/J.TCRβ−/−)52 (Fig. 6A). Following transfer, we found kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells in mice receiving CD8 T cells alone or CD8+CD4 T cells (Fig. 6B). Transfer of CD8+CD4 T cells, but not of CD8 or CD4 T cells alone, resulted in kidney injury (Fig. 6C). In absence of CD4 T cells, stem-like CD8 T cells in the kidney retained Ly108 expression, indicating that CD4 T cells direct CD8 T cell differentiation from a stem-like into an effector state to cause tissue injury (Fig. S6A). This injury was autoantibody-independent, as transfer of CD4 T cells alone did not increase the protein:creatinine ratio despite IgG and complement (C3) deposition in the kidney (Fig. 6D,E; S6B), consistent with CD4 T cell-dependence of pathogenic autoantibody production in lupus53. These data demonstrated that CD4 T cells promote CD8 T cell effector function in lupus nephritis to drive kidney injury.

### Kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells require IL-15 and IL-21 signaling for effector function and kidney injury

We speculated that kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells required CD4 T cell help through cytokines, parallel to requirements for cytotoxic CD8 T cell function in cancer and viral infections54–58. We merged CD4 and CD8 T cell multiome datasets (Fig. 6F) and performed unbiased intercellular communication analysis using Scriabin59 to uncover interaction between ligand-expressing ‘sender’ cells and receptor-expressing ‘receiver’ cells. Two interaction programs, Cd40lg-Cd40 and Cd80-Cd28, indicated direct contact between kidney-infiltrating CD4 and CD8 T cells (Fig. S6C). Given that CD40 signaling supports CD8 T cell expansion, effector function, and memory formation60–62, and that CD80 on activated T cells can deliver CD28-dependent co-stimulation to partner T cells63–66, these interaction programs supports CD4-CD8 co-stimulatory interactions. Beyond this co-stimulatory axis, we identified Il21 ligand-expressing ‘sender’ CD4 Tfh cells interacting with Il21r and Il2rg-expressing ‘receiver’ CD8 T cells (Fig. 6G) with Il21 ligand activity most prominent in cytotoxic CD8 T cells (Fig. S6D). We also identified Ifng, Il10, and Tnf-ligand expressing “sender” CD4 T cells, interacting with Ifngr1, Il10ra, and Tnfrsf1b-expressing ‘receiver’ CD8 T cells, respectively (Fig. S6E–G)

We next asked if cytokines produced by other cells could also support differentiation of stem-like to effector CD8 T cells. IL-15 production by kidney parenchymal cells67 and myeloid cells68 occurs in proinflammatory environments. While we were unable to detect Il15 in CD4 T cells (Fig. S6H), Il15ra was readily detected on CD8 T cells (Fig. 6H), and progressively increased as CD8 T cells differentiated (Fig. 6I), indicating de novo synthesis of the IL-15Rα subunit rather than acquisition from ancillary cells. In a like manner, IL-21R expression increased with activation (Fig. 6I). Expression of Il15ra (Fig. 6H) and Il21r (Fig. 6G) overlapped with expression of Gzmb (Fig. S6I), implicating IL-15 and IL-21 as drivers of cytotoxic CD8 T cell formation. Accordingly, in vitro exposure of stem-like CD8 T cells to different cytokine combinations showed that IL-15 and IL-21 primarily drove granzyme B expression (Fig. S6J).

We next applied NicheNet69 to predicted ligand-response genes in kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cell subsets. Ifng and Il21 (Fig. S6K) and Il15 and Il21 (Fig 6J) signaling in kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells predicted upregulation of genes associated with activation, effector function, migration, and survival across CD8 T cell subsets. Notably, Gzmb expression was exclusively downstream of combined Il15 and Il21 signaling, suggesting a synergistic effect in driving CD8 T cytotoxicity. Accordingly, we observed significant production of granzyme B upon stimulation of stem-like CD8 T cells with IL-15 and IL-21, further enhanced by TCR-stimulation (Fig. 6K), as previously reported70,71. This functionally enabled killing of parenchymal kidney cells (Fig. 6L). These findings emphasize the role of local cytokines in shaping kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cell differentiation, survival, and cytotoxic function.

We also investigated the role of type I IFN, associated with nephritis72 and found that exposure of stem-like CD8 T cells to type I IFN drove upregulation of both IL-15Rα and IL-21R (Fig. S6L). Thus, as stem-like cells enter the type I interferon rich nephritic kidney microenvironment73,74, they become primed for IL-15 and IL-21 signaling to drive cytotoxicity.

To determine whether IL-15 or IL-21 blockade protected kidneys from injury, we adoptively transferred CD8+CD4 T cells into MRL/lpr TCRβ−/− mice, then treated with anti-IL-21R and/or anti-CD122 (IL-2Rβ subunit) to block IL-15 signaling75,76 using clone 5H4 which inhibits binding of IL-15 but not of IL-2 to the subunit77 (Fig. 6M). After treatment, we observed a significant reduction in the number of kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells with all three treatment conditions, with a synergistic effect when combining anti-CD122 and anti-IL-21R (Fig. 6N, S6M–O). Following treatment, kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells retained TCF-1 expression with diminished granzyme B expression (Fig. 6O), reflective of inhibited differentiation from stem-like to cytotoxic CD8 T cells. Accordingly, PD-1+Tim-3+ cells were decreased (Fig. 6P), and urinary protein:creatinine and interstitial infiltration were reduced (Fig. 6Q,R), indicating protective effect against tissue injury following IL-15 and/or IL-21 blockade.

### Stem-like CD8 T cell differentiation pathways are conserved in patients with lupus nephritis

To draw parallels with human disease, we analyzed biopsies from 156 lupus nephritis patients and 30 healthy donor controls profiled using scRNA-sequencing. We identified 34,736 T and NK cells, which clustered into stem-like, tissue-resident memory, GZMK+, and cytotoxic CD8 T cells; stemlike, Th1, Treg, Th17, Tfh/Tph, and memory CD4 T cells; NK cells; γδ T cells; ISG-high cells, and ILCs (Fig. 7A,B; S7A).

Cytotoxic and GZMK+ clusters were enriched in patient biopsies compared to healthy controls, highlighting the key role of CD8 T cells in nephritic kidneys (Fig. 7C). Assessment of stemness based on expression of TCF7, LEF1, CCR7, IL7R, BACH2, and SLAMF6 identified several stem-like clusters (Fig. 7D). We applied Diffusion Mapping to determine trajectory along pseudotime and found a stem-like CD8 T cell cluster (T4) is precursor to cytotoxic (Fig. 7E,G) and tissue-resident memory CD8 T cells (Fig. 7F,H). In human CD8 T cells, GZMK expression rises along the course of cytotoxic CD8 T cell differentiation, denoting an intermediary state78,79. In line with this, we observed a reciprocal relationship between clusters expressing GZMB and GZMK (Fig. 7I). We also identified a common CD4 T cell stem-like precursor (cluster T8) that gave rise to kidney-infiltrating Th1, Tfh, Treg, and Th17 subsets. (Fig. S7B–E).

To understand how these cells changed with disease progression, we applied co-varying neighborhood analysis80 (CNA) along disease chronicity index, a measure of the extent of irreversible kidney damage that is expected to increase during disease33,81,82. CNA suggested a higher chronicity index is associated with an increase in the relative frequency of stem-like CD8 T cells and a decrease in that of cytotoxic CD8 T cells (Fig. 7J; S7F). The negative correlation between the chronicity index and cytotoxic CD8 T cell frequency remained significant when factoring in patient race, ethnicity, sex, age, time of biopsy, lupus nephritis class, and treatment (Table S1). We did not observe independent correlation between cytotoxic CD8 T cells and disease activity, ISN class, or treatment response (Fig. S7G–I).

### IL-15 and IL-21 drive cytotoxic CD8 T cell pathways in patients with lupus nephritis

To test whether IL-15 and IL-21 drive kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cell cytotoxicity in human lupus nephritis, we used Scriabin and NicheNet to infer CD4-CD8 intracellular communications using gene expression from kidney biopsies. We identified significant CD40LG-CD40 and CD80-CD28 interactions that support CD4-CD8 co-stimulation (Fig. S7J). We also identified IL21 ligand-expressing ‘sender’ CD4 Tfh/Tph cells engaged IL21R-expressing ‘receiver’ CD8 T cells (Fig. S7K), with strongest IL-21 signaling in late effector CD8 T cells (Fig. S7M). Our data also revealed an IL-15-IL15RA interaction program, with IL15RA readily detected in ‘receiver’ CD8 T cells (Fig. S7L), whereas IL15 expression was negligible in CD4 and CD8 T cells, implicating a non-T source for IL-15 production, as in mice. Finally, as in mice, IL15 and IL21 were predicted to synergistically drive GZMB expression in early and late kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells (Fig. S7N), an effect captured in by in vitro culture of patient, but not healthy donor CD8 T cells, with IL-15 and IL-21 (Fig. S7O). Together, these findings highlight parallel IL-21 and IL-15-driven cytotoxicity in nephritic kidneys from human and mice.

## DISCUSSION

Lupus nephritis is considered a consequence of autoantibody production and immune complex deposition in the kidney leading to parenchymal injury1. In lupus nephritis patient biopsies, the presence of kidney-infiltrating immune cells is the strongest predictor of poor clinical outcome, with CD8 T cell presence predictive of progression to kidney failure11,13–15. Here, we established a central role for kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells in driving kidney injury through direct cell killing of kidney parenchymal cells.

We considered how kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells arise and are maintained, drawing parallels from chronic infection and cancer, settings of chronic antigen exposure in which progenitor CD8 T cells with capacity to self-renew replenish dysfunctional effector counterparts25,30,83. We found TCF-1+ stem-like cells in rLN and spleens of lupus prone mice that gave rise to granzyme B-expressing cells with capacity to cause tissue injury in both mice and humans with lupus nephritis. In chronic infection and cancer, stem-like CD8 T cells that replenish the effector cell pool after chronic antigen stimulation lead to viral or tumor eradication25,26,31, but in autoimmune disease this results in injury to self-tissue. Indeed, such a program is operative for CD884,85 and CD486,87 T cells in organ-specific autoimmunity models. These findings have not heretofore been demonstrated in systemic autoimmune diseases. While kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells have evidence of dysfunction in the murine lupus kidney88, their replenishment from a stem-like pool with effector differentiation and adaptation to the tissue environment nonetheless leads to progressive organ injury18.

Where do kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells originate? If our comparison to other chronic antigen models is applicable31,89,90, then draining lymph nodes would be the source from which stem-like CD8 T cells are supplied to kidneys. In support of this, TCR signaling genes were enriched in rLN CD8 T cells but not those in the spleen, and expanded CD8 T cell clones exhibited stepwise expansion starting from rLNs, through the spleen, with maximal expansion in the kidney. Accordingly, we observed Nr4a1 expression downstream of TCR signaling in rLNs and kidneys but not spleens. In both FTY720 and CD8 depletion experiments, stem-like cells in the kidney continued to differentiate. Taken together, these results indicated that stem-like CD8 T cells bridge lymphoid tissue and the kidneys, after which they differentiate in the kidney. In support of this conclusion, we observed kidney infiltration only after transferring stem-like CD8 T cells from rLNs but not upon transfer of more differentiated cells.

What is the nature of the CD8 T cell response and is it directed against self-antigens? We generated a Nur77-eGFP reporter mouse on a lupus-prone genetic background to allow us to determine whether TCR engagement drove CD8 T cell function, as a proxy for antigen-driven responses. We observed increased clonal expansion of kidney-infiltrating eGFP+CD8 T cells, which expressed higher granzyme B despite terminal differentiation, consistent with a chronic autoantigen-driven response present in kidneys. Granzyme B expression is primarily dictated by TCR signaling, replacing granzyme K, which is tonically expressed in CD8 T cells under inflammatory states secondary to cytokine stimulation91–93. As multiple cell types, including renal glomerular and tubular cells, are damaged in lupus nephritis94, it is likely that the T cell autoantigenic targets are broad. To this point, expanded TCR clones were unique to individual mice, mirroring previous findings95, suggesting multiple T cell target antigens and/or stochasticity of initial T cell activation.

CD8 T cell differentiation in cancer and chronic infection leads to upregulation of immune checkpoint molecules and diminished effector function. While we observed similar upregulation of these molecules, we did not see a corresponding decrease in effector function, suggesting that in lupus, kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cell effector function fails to terminate. AP-1 signaling remained prominent despite terminal differentiation, which, taken alongside Nur77 expression, indicated that TCR-mediated responses towards kidney antigens sustain CD8 T cell effector function.

Regulation of CD8 T cell effector function balances protective cellular responses and minimizing damage to host tissue. Separation of progenitor CD8 T cells from target tissue achieves this, effectively limiting the number of cells arising within the tissue when the source is interrupted, as we observed herein. A second layer of CD8 T cell regulation necessitates the help of CD4 T cells for differentiation and function54–56,58. We found a parallel requirement of CD4 T cell help in driving tissue injury by CD8 T cells, as stem-like CD8 T cells had impaired differentiation in the absence of CD4 T cells. The nature of this help evolved over time, but featured IFNγ, IL-21, IL-10, and TNF-α, all of which have been described as central for CD8 T cell differentiation and function96–99.

Cytokines produced by other cells also play prominent roles in CD8 T cell differentiation, function, and survival. Kidney-infiltrating CD8 T cells expressed IL-15Rα as they differentiated and in response to type I IFN. IL-15 promotes CD8 T cell maintenance and cytotoxic function100,101. We found that IL-15 synergized with IL-21 to drive granzyme B production from stem-like CD8 T cell precursors, an effect enhanced by TCR signaling, with their blockade ameliorating kidney injury. This finding reinforced the idea that cytotoxic CD8 T cell generation within the kidney occurs from stem-like precursors that are exposed to kidney antigens in a permissive local cytokine environment.

We propose an expanded model in which lupus nephritis is initiated by autoantibody deposition and immune cell trafficking into the kidney, including stem-like CD8 T cells which originate from the rLN. In the kidney, stem-like CD8 T cells clonally expand and differentiate to cause antigen-specific tissue injury, dependent upon IL-21 from CD4 T cells and IL-15. This model mirrors checkpoint inhibitor therapy in cancer, in which stem-like precursors from draining lymph nodes continuously reinforce tumors to drive eradication102. In systemic autoimmunity, however, we posit this cycle is detrimental, leading to progressive tissue injury, consistent with findings showing that a high stem-like signature predicts poor SLE prognosis103.

These findings do not rule out pathogenicity of other cells and instead complements roles of other immune cells. B cells are implicated in lupus pathogenesis, with their targeting a therapeutic mainstay6,10,104. However, circulating autoantibodies in lupus nephritis patients are found several years prior to symptom onset and do not always lead to disease5. Our findings suggest that B cells contribute to lupus pathogenesis beyond their production of pathogenic autoantibodies. They cross-present antigens105,106 and instruct CD4 T cells to provide local production of IL-2157. Such B cell helper function, however, is likely redundant with other immune cells, explaining why current B cell depleting antibodies fail to provide therapeutic benefit in over half of patients. Further work is needed to untangle the role of B cells and other cells in instructing CD8 T cell function in lupus nephritis and how CAR-T cell directed B cell depletion may affect disease remission104.

Myeloid cells and macrophages contribute to the pathogenesis of lupus nephritis, with pro-inflammatory then tissue repair gene signatures mirroring disease progression toward chronicity107,108. We explored changes of CD8 T cells along disease progression, finding that stem-like CD8 T cells positively correlated with disease chronicity, while cytotoxic CD8 T cells had an inverse relationship. Upon modeling the differentiation trajectory from stem-like to cytotoxic CD8 T cells, we suggest a positive feedback loop in which the rate of differentiation from stem-like CD8 T cells is an increasing function of the number of cytotoxic CD8 T cells. With more cytotoxic CD8 T cells, this rate of differentiation is higher. Upon decrease in cytotoxic cell number (e.g., cell death or treatment), the latter rate would also decrease, with consequent accumulation of stem-like CD8 T cells. By contrast, a negative feedback loop in which differentiation rate is a decreasing function of the number of cytotoxic cells cannot explain this observation, and neither can a simple increase in the rate in which stem-like CD8 T cells enter the kidney since this would lead to an increase in all CD8 T cell subsets.

These findings allow for re-thinking of systemic autoimmunity as embedded localized responses distinct from those occurring systemically. Understanding these distinctions enables additional therapeutic interventions for SLE as the prototypical systemic autoimmune syndrome.

## LIMITATIONS OF THE STUDY

Our ability to assess antigen specificity in this study was limited, as antigen(s) driving kidney injury in murine lupus are unknown. This is unlike investigation of organ-specific autoimmune diseases, cancer, and chronic infection that utilize TCR transgenic T cells or tetramer-defined antigen-specific cells. MRL/lpr mice are Fas deficient, which would obscure Fas-mediated killing. While we observed enrichment in cytotoxic CD8 T cells in kidney biopsies in lupus nephritis, tissue histology among samples was heterogeneous, including pure membranous, proliferative, and mixed lupus nephritis subsets109. Patients received different treatments, potentially confounding interpretation. Our analysis of human samples was also limited to kidney tissue per se as we did not determine immune responses in lymphoid organs.

## METHODS

### EXPERIMENTAL MODEL AND STUDY PARTICIPANT DETAILS

#### Mice

MRL/MpJ-Faslpr/J (MRL/lpr), NZBW/F1J, and B6.Sle1.Yaa mice were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory (stock #000485, #100008, #021569, respectively) and sacrificed at 12–16, 30–36 weeks, 16–20 weeks, respectively. MRL/lpr.Nur77-eGFP reporters were generated by crossing MRL/MpJ-Faslpr/J with B6N.B6-Tg(Nr4a1-EGFP/cre)820Khog/J (The Jackson Laboratory stock #018974). MRL/MpJ-Faslpr/J.TCRβ−/− were generated from a prior study52. Male and female mice were used for all strains except B6.Sle1.Yaa, in which only male mice were used as female mice do not develop disease. Littermate controls were used for treatment experiments. All animals were maintained in a specific pathogen-free facility at Yale School of Medicine. All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care & Use Committee (IACUC).

#### Human PBMC processing and CD8 T cell isolation

Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were obtained from peripheral venous blood collected from lupus patients under protocols approved by the institutional review board (IRB), with written informed consent from all participants. Control PBMCs were obtained from age and sex-matched healthy donors. Whole blood was collected into sodium heparin coated tubes and processed within 4–8 hours of phlebotomy. PBMCs were isolated by density-gradient centrifugation using Histopaque (Sigma-Aldrich). Following centrifugation, the mononuclear cell layer was carefully filtered, washed twice in Dulbecco’s phosphate-buffered saline (DPBS). Cell viability was assessed using tryptan blue exclusion. PBMCs were cryopreserved in fetal bovine serum (FBS) supplemented with 10% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and stored in liquid nitrogen until further use.

### METHOD DETAILS

#### Cell preparation and flow cytometry

Mice were intravenously injected with anti-CD45.1 or CD45.2 for 5 minutes before sacrifice for labeling of circulating lymphocytes110. Kidneys were then harvested, capsules were mechanically removed, mashed, and digested in RPMI-1640 containing 10% FBS, 100IU/mL collagenase D, 2mM CaCl2, and 2mM MgCl2 or 45 minutes at 37°C. Following enzymatic digestion, single cell suspension was obtained using gentleMACS and filtration through a 70 μm strainer. Cells were resuspended in PBS and lymphocytes were enriched by Ficoll density gradient. Spleens and bilateral renal lymph nodes were harvested, mashed, and filtered through 70μm strainers in PBS followed by RBC lysis. For surface staining, single cell suspension was incubated with antibodies at 4°C in PBS for 30 minutes. For intracellular staining, cells were processed with Foxp3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer Set (eBioscience). Live/dead cell stains were used to ensure comparable viability across tissue. Cells were analyzed using LSR II flow cytometer (BD Bioscience) or FACSymphony cell analyzer (BD Bioscience) or sorted using FACSAria (BD Bioscience). Data were analyzed by FlowJo software v10.8.1.

#### CD8 T cell depletion

8-week-old MRL/MpJ-Faslpr/J mice were intraperitoneally treated with 1mg/kg Ultra-LEAF™ Purified anti-mouse CD8α (BioLegend) or Ultra-LEAF™ Purified Rat IgG2a, κ Isotype Ctrl (BioLegend) every 4 days for 9 total treatments. Urine and serum were collected from mice prior to and at the end of treatment.

#### PD-1 inhibition

8-week-old MRL/MpJ-Faslpr/J mice were intraperitoneally treated with 250ug anti-PD-1 (BioXCell) twice a week for 8 weeks.

#### Measurement of anti-dsDNA antibodies

Anti-dsDNA antibodies in mouse serum were measured on Nunc PolySorp 96 well plates (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coated with calf thymus DNA (MilliporeSigma) in Reacti-BindTM buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Alkaline phosphatase-conjugated anti-mouse IgG antibodies (SouthernBiotech) and phosphatase substrate (MilliporeSigma) were used for detection. ODs were read at 405nm on a SpectraMax Microplate Reader (Molecular Devices).

#### 10x single-cell multiomic analysis (paired RNA-seq and ATAC-seq)

Single-cell-sorted activated (CD44hi) T cells form kidney, spleen, and renal lymph node of six 14wk-old lupus-prone MRL/MpJ-Faslpr/J mice were resuspended in FACS Buffers (PBS + 0.5% HI-FBS) before proceeding to single-cell sample preparation. Nuclei suspensions were prepared using the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression (GEX) protocol (10x Genomics). Lysis time was optimized as 4 minutes on ice for activated T cells. Centrifuge steps were conducted as 500 rcf for 5 minutes at 4°C. Nuclei samples were resuspended in Diluted Nuclei Buffer and counted with hemocytometer prior to sample loading onto the 10x Genomics Chromium platform.

#### 10x Multiome library preparation and sequencing

GEX and ATAC libraries were sequenced on a NovaSeq system using HiSeq paired-end 150bp by Yale Center for Genome Analysis (YCGA). Prepared nuclei were loaded onto Chromium Next GEM chip with a target final barcoded nuclei recovery of approximately 20,000. A single GEM generation and barcoding assay was performed for prepared nuclei from each tissue (cells from different mice pooled) to generate independent ATAC and RNA cDNA libraries. The final libraries were quantified using a Qubit dsDNA HS Assay Kit (Invitrogen) and a High Sensitivity D1000 DNA kit on Agilent 2200 TapeStation system. Kidney and renal lymph node cDNA libraries were then sequenced on NovaSeq 6000 S4 flow cell. From kidneys, we recovered 12,872 barcoded nuclei that passed CellRanger knee call, 32,677 ATAC read pairs, and 23,778 RNA read pairs per nuclei. From renal lymph nodes, we recovered 3,423 barcoded nuclei that passed CellRanger knee call, 170,799 ATAC read pairs, and 108,591 RNA read pairs per nuclei. From spleens, we recovered > 20,000 barcoded nuclei that passed CellRanger knee call, 45,366 ATAC read pairs, and 51,011 RNA read pairs per nuclei.

#### Determining ATAC and RNA counts from 10X Multiome data

Raw fastq sequences from Chromium Single Cell Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression sequencing (ATAC & RNA) were demultiplexed with CellRanger-Arc v2 (10x Genomics) mkfastq and sequences were aligned to mm10 reference genome reference genome CellRanger-Arc count. Cell barcodes that passed knee call by CellRanger-Arc were used for downstream analyses.

#### Removal of low-quality cells and doublets

Cells that passed knee call were used to construct filtered feature count matrices to initialize independent RNA and ATAC Seurat Objects111,112 per tissue sample. Cell barcodes in RNA Seurat objects were filtered to remove cells with ≥ 7.5% mitochondrial gene content, ≤ 200 genes, and RNA UMI counts ≤ 500 or ≥ 50,000. Cell barcodes in ATAC Seurat objects were filtered to remove cells with ≤ 200 unique ATAC fragments, nucleosome signal strength ≥ 1, TSS enrichment score ≤ 2, and ATAC UMI counts ≤ 350 or ≥ 30,000. Filtered RNA and ATAC Seurat Objects were then merged by shared GEX cell barcode ID. To remove doublets, we applied scDblFinder113, which calculated expected doublet rates and identified heterotypic doublets from cellular RNA content by comparing cellular transcriptome against artificially simulated doublets.

#### Exclusion of naïve CD8 T cells

We included B6 naïve cells from the spleen95 into our bioinformatic analysis to exclude potential contamination by naïve cells. Cells were reclustered following batch correction and incorporation into spleen, renal lymph node, and kidney datasets, with naïve cells clustering distinctly from all CD44hi cells in our analysis.

#### ATAC data processing (refining peak calls, data normalization, transcription factor and gene locus chromatin accessibility)

ATAC peaks called by CellRanger-Arc were recalled using MACS2 v2.2.7.1114 with default parameters in Signac v1.7115. MACS2 recalled ATAC peaks were normalized by latent semantic indexing [LSI: term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) followed by singular value decomposition (SVD)] in Signac v1.7 to correct for differences in cellular sequencing depth and across all peaks and to assign higher values to rare peaks. Gene accessibility was measured in Signac v1.7 (determined as number of fragments mapping to each gene locus extended by 2kb upstream region to include promoter). Gene accessibility data was normalized by LogNormalize in Seurat v5 to adjust for gene accessibility measurements by the total accessibility in each cell multiplied by median UMI (scale factor = median UMI count), and then scaled by ScaleData (expression distribution of each gene feature across cells is transformed to a centered mean of 0 and feature’s scaled expression in each cell is represented as standard deviations from the mean). Chromatin accessibility at gene locus was visualized by CoveragePlot in Signac v1.7. Peak coordinates were assigned to genes by ClosestFeature in Signac v1.7 with reference genome mm10. Transcription factor accessibility was measured in Z-scores deviations computed using chromVAR v1.18116 with mouse genome reference mm10 and transcription factor binding motif references from the JASPAR2022 Core Vertebrates database117.

#### RNA data normalization

RNA data was normalized by LogNormalize (feature expression measurement divided by the total expression in each cell multiplied by a scale factor of 10,000 then natural log transformed) in Seurat v5. Top 2000 variable genes were determined using FindVariableFeatures with ‘vst’ selection method, and the normalized RNA data was scaled for variable genes using ScaleData.

#### Batch effect correction for combined tissue data

For tissue-combined datasets, we corrected for batch effect for each ATAC and RNA assay to account for technical variation from separate 10x runs. To correct for batch effects between ATAC datasets, we performed integration by identifying pairwise anchors (pairwise correspondences between single cells across datasets) using FindIntegrationAnchors in Seurat v5 with reciprocal LSI reduction method. The reciprocal LSI coordinates were then integrated across ATAC dataset using IntegrateEmbeddings. To correct for batch effects between RNA datasets, we performed PCA dimensionality reduction followed by integration by Harmony118.

#### ATAC and RNA integration, data visualization, and cell cluster generation

To identify and visualize cell subsets for each tissue and for combined tissue datasets, we integrated independently processed ATAC and RNA modalities by performing weighted-nearest neighbor (WNN) analysis. Twenty nearest neighbors for each cell were calculated based on the weighted combination of ATAC and RNA profile similarities using FindMultiModalNeighbors in Seurat v5, with integrated ATAC LSI embeddings and harmony as dimensional reductions (2:30, 1:35 numbers of components, respectively). Next, we used the WNN knn outputs in RunUMAP in Seurat v5 to visualize cells in 2D space by Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)119. Then, the weighted nearest neighbors dimension reduction was used in cluster determination in Seurat v5 with the SLM algorithm at an optimal resolution parameter of 0.5 as determined by Clustree evaluation120 and visualized by UMAP.

#### T cell subset identification

CD4 T cells and CD8 T cells were determined from each tissue dataset by expressions of RNA markers (CD3e, Cd4, and Cd8a) and subsetted out as independent Seurat objects. Next, for CD4 and CD8 T cell datasets, and for tissue-combined T cell dataset, we re-processed the Seurat Objects. First, we removed all Mitochondrial Mt genes, B cell Ig and Jchain genes, and Ribosomal protein Rpl and Rps genes to mitigate background noise when generating T cell specific clusters. Next, we re-performed MACS2 peak call, determination of transcription factor motif accessibility and chromatin accessibility at gene locus, counts data normalization and scaling, batch effect correction, WNN integration using integrated ATAC LSI embeddings and harmony components, data visualization by WNN UMAP, and cell cluster generation. Next, for CD4 and CD8 T cell datasets, we manually annotated each determined clusters by averaged expression of key cell subset-defining genes and transcription factor binding motif accessibility (by chromVAR). For tissue-combined dataset, cell subset annotation labels were transferred over from tissue-specific T cell datasets.

#### Analyses of differential gene expression, chromatin accessibility at gene locus and peak, and transcription factor accessibility

Differential expression analyses were performed using FindMarkers (comparisons of 2 groups) or FindAllMarkers (comparisons of > 2 groups) in Seurat v5, with the following feature selection filters: 1) minimum percent of cells expressing the feature threshold (min.pct) and 2) log2 fold change or average difference threshold (logfc.threshold), as specified in figure legends for each comparison. As intended by Seurat V5, only features that met ‘min.pct’ and ‘logfc.threshold’ cutoffs were retained for comparisons, so that rarely expressed genes or genes having low differential expression (low effect size) do not skew the differential expression results (i.e., the FDR-adjusted P value). Of note, no min.pct values were set for differential chromVAR scores since they are Z-scores.

For differential gene accessibility, normalized and scaled data was used to determine fold change significance, with Wilcoxon Rank-sum test as method for fold change significance. For differential peak accessibility, normalized and scaled data was used to determine fold change significance, with logistic regression as method for fold change significance. For differential peak accessibility and RNA expression, normalized and scaled data was used to determine fold change significance, with Wilcoxon Rank-sum test as method for fold change significance. For differential transcription factor motif accessibility analyses, Z-score data was used to determine mean differences in accessibility deviations, with Wilcoxon Rank-sum test as method for significant difference.

For heatmaps and dot plot representations of averaged feature expression of significantly differentially expressed features, averaged feature expression were calculated using normalized and feature-level scaled values so that all feature expressions can be shown on the same Z-score scale. This scaling is applied for all averaged feature expressions shown in heatmaps and dot plots (RNA, accessibility), except for transcription factor motif accessibility (which were already in Z-score).

#### Pseudo-time trajectory analysis

Branched pseudotime trajectories were built by sequentially selecting precursor cells with the highest similarity in chromatin accessibility landscape as learned by Monocle v342 to build branched pseudo-time trajectories. First, Seurat object was converted to CellDataSet (CDS) object. Then, each cell is clustered and partitioned to learn whether cells belonged in the same trajectory (cluster) or separate trajectories (partition) by cluster_cells with WNN UMAP dimensionality reduction and Louvain cluster method. Within each partition, per-cell chromatin accessibility variation is generalized and fitted on a principal graph by learn_graph, and the principal curve established a reference curve that represented the magnitude of pseudotime score difference from any two reference points (cells) within a partition. Next, cells were ordered in pseudotime by order_cell, and the root node (trajectory beginning) was set to stem-like T cells. This settled the 0-point reference to adjust pseudo-time scores of all cells along the principal curve.

To determine dynamic changes in transcription factor motif accessibility, gene accessibility, and gene expression along a trajectory (e.g., from stem-like to terminally differentiated), cells along that path in the principal graph (e.g., stem-like to terminally differentiated) was subsetted by choose_graph_segments from the CDS object. Next, the Seurat object was subsetted for the same cells by matched barcode ID, and the pseudotime scores was transferred from the CDS object to the Seurat object. Cells were then ordered by pseudotime scores and binned into 10 subgroups to determine significantly differentially accessible transcription factor binding motifs, gene accessibility, and gene expression. Finally, heatmap was applied to visualize per-cell expressions for significant features identified for cells ranked by pseudotime score.

Note that trajectory topology and directionality depend on manual root and path selection. Single-cell chromatin accessibility is also susceptible to technical sparsity of ATAC-seq. Thus, the inferred progression from stem-like to terminally differentiated cell states should be interpreted with caution.

#### Pathway enrichment analysis by Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)

All 31,614 mouse genes were ranked by log2 fold change in gene expression comparisons between kidney and other (LN and spleen) CD8 T cells. Gene ranks were used to determine significantly enriched gene sets in kidney using fGSEA v1.22 with default settings121. Reference gene sets were retrieved from MSigDB v2022.1122,123 using msigdbr v7.5.1124. Specifically, a total of 111,634 reference gene sets from the H (hallmark), C2 (curated), and C7 (immunologic signature) collections were retrieved from MSigDB. Gene sets were considered significantly enriched with P < 0.05. P values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method.

#### Gene module identification by WGCNA

Co-expressed gene programs (modules) were discovered through Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA)43 as previously described125. Briefly, Seurat object was subset by cells of interest and the expression matrix of 50 genes most positively and negatively associated with the first < 10 principal components were used as input for WGCNA v1.70126. A soft power was selected as recommended where possible125: the first power with a scale-free topology > 0.8, but this soft power was reduced if fewer than 3 modules with a minimum gene size of 10 were identified. The vectorized topological overlap matrix (TOM) dissimilarity matrix was compared with 10,000 randomly generated and vectorized TOM dissimilarity matrices from the same gene list used for module discovery. Module was determined as significant if FDR-adjusted P < 0.05 (one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test) in at least 95% of 10,000 permutation tests. Similar modules were merged using a dissimilarity threshold of 0.5 (MEDissThres = 0.5). To visualize gene pair co-expression, 31,614 × 31,614 mouse gene pair Pearson’s correlation coefficients were determined using the corSparse function in qlcMatrix R package. For list of genes identified in WGCNA gene modules, we made a custom script to generate a pairwise gene expression Pearson’s correlation coefficient heatmap for cells in each condition. Condition-specific heatmaps were merged along the diagonal split (highlighted in black) to provide a visual contrast of the degree of gene pair co-expression in each of the two conditions being compared.

#### Constructing gene regulatory network

Gene regulatory network was constructed by linking gene expression – peak accessibility (gene – peak) associations to gene expression – transcription factor (gene – TF) motif accessibility associations for CD8 T cell datasets across organs using FigR127. First, Spearman correlation between gene expression and chromatin accessibility of gene’s transcriptional start site (TSS) was computed for each gene and compared against correlation between the same gene to 100 background peaks with matching GC content and accessibility by permutation test. Then, genes with at least 3 significant peak – gene associations (by correlation between gene expression and TSS chromatin accessibility) were determined as domains of regulatory chromatin (DORCs). Next, we performed cisTopic128 to determine optimal numbers of cis-regulatory topics (by log-likelihood) from ATAC counts data, which represents sets of chromatin regions that contribute to cell and cell cluster identity. For gene accessibility and gene expression of DORC genes, smoothing was applied to sparse counts data per feature per cell using K nearest neighbors (KNNs) derived from cell – cisTopic probability distributions.

To determine TF to gene associations for DORC genes, the Spearman correlation coefficient between TF gene expression and DORC gene expression was computed for all TFs whose binding motifs were enriched in DORC accessible peaks by runFigRGRN, using built-in reference TF motif database and smoothed DORC gene accessibility and RNA count matrix. Mean regulation scores (signed, −log10 scaled TF-gene Spearman correlation) were computed to predict activator (positive regulation score) and repressor (negative regulation score) TFs on DORC gene expression. Finally, transcription factors were ranked as putative activators or repressors TFs by rankDrivers, which computes a signed meanScore representing the average of motif enrichment Z-score and TF-DORC correlation.

#### Cell-cell communication determination

Scriabin59 Interaction Program analysis was performed to determine significant cell-cell ligand-receptor pairs between CD4 T cell and CD8 T cell subsets. After significant ligand – receptor interactions were determined for specific T cell subsets, Scriabin’s implementation of NicheNet129 was performed to determine ligand activity in receptor expressing cell types by RNA expression of predicted gene responses due to ligand – receptor interactions.

We performed differential ligand – receptor interaction analysis across tissue-specific CD4 T and CD8 T cells, using sparse RNA count matrix of combined tissue-specific CD4 T cell and CD8 T cell Seurat object, to identify interaction programs (modules of co-expressed ligand-receptor pairs) by FindAllInteractionPrograms in Scriabin, with ‘assay’ set to RNA, J’accard overlap index threshold’ set to 0.4 for interaction program merging, ‘species’ set to mouse, ligand and receptor database set to OmniPath130, and group.by set to ‘T cell subsets’ so that cells from each tissue-specific T cells subset are equally represented in the subsamples used for iterative approximations of ligand – receptor pair topological overlap matrix. For all interaction programs determined, significance of each interaction program was tested by InteractionProgramSignificance, which compares the ligand – receptor co-expression in each program against 10,000 randomly generated interaction programs (Mann-Whitney U test, less than 500 p > 0.05 for significant programs). Next, per cell scores were calculated for all significant interaction programs using ScoreInteractionPrograms in Scriabin. For each significant interaction program, sender (ligand expressing, blue) and receiver (receptor expressing, red) cells were visualized in WNN UMAP plot by IPFeaturePlot.

Scriabin implementation of NicheNet was performed to determine ligand activity in receiver cells by RNA expression of predicted gene responses, using NicheNet database of predicted gene expression changes due to specific ligand – receptor interactions. To determine most active ligands in receiver cell types by expression levels of response genes, cellular RNA expression data was used to determine variable genes in T cell subsets (IDVariantGenes, ‘group.by’ set to T cell subsets), generate gene signature for ligand activity ranking (GenerateCellSignature, default settings), and predict ligand activity using cell-resolved gene signatures (RankActiveLigands, default settings).
